responseDecisions.3.2: Preserved original three-plus-two finding sequence and closing positions; separated involuntary influences from chosen procedures and added concrete test requirements.
responseDecisions.4.1: Preserved seven questions/seven end keys; corrected evidentialism and neuroscience questions, bounded indirect-influence question and separated options visually.
responseDecisions.4.2: Preserved seven questions/seven end keys; removed complete-control overstatement, ambiguous confirmation-bias answer and inference from emotion to wholesale involuntarism.
responseDecisions.5.1: Retained ten of twelve questions verbatim; revised neuroscience and intervention questions to stop presupposing what experiments prove.
responseDecisions.5.2: Retained eight of twelve questions verbatim; sharpened responsibility, feed, motivated-reasoning and experimental-design questions without assuming total control or guaranteed bias elimination.

research.use: McHugh alternative control account; repository abstract retrieved in search, direct open errored.
Original experiments; cognitive load/time pressure finding and authors’ interpretation, bounded to tasks.

source.title: The Burden of Proof
allPromptTexts: I understand the burden of proof to be the social obligation of someone who makes a public claim to substantiate that claim. Is this definition correct, or is it wrong or incomplete?
How might a burden of proof scenario arise in the context of scientific inquiry?
Can you provide an actual scenario in which a burden of proof arose from a scientific inquiry?
Can you expound on the difference you implied between evidence and substantiation?
Can you instantiate your bridge analogy with an actual scenario?

In public discourse, we often encounter arguments over who has the burden of proof. In a case in which one person claims Elvis is still alive and the other claims he is dead, who actually bears the burden of proof? Provide an in-depth elaboration on this scenario.

I am going to gently tread into more controversial territory. Please apply the same principles you used in the Elvis scenario above to the following. If one person claims a miraculous God exists, and their interlocutor claims such a God does not exist, who has the burden of proof?
How can we best respond to someone who makes a claim, and then hands us the burden of proof to demonstrate their claim is false.
Create a 5-item quiz based on the discussion above with answers at the end.
Provide 12 discussion questions relevant to the content above.

responseDecisions.1.1: Reviewed definition plus two embedded follow-up responses; retained all prompt positions, five-stage science list and three-paragraph Copernican example. Corrected burden/standard, evidence/falsifiability, peer-review/replication and Venus/Tycho distinctions.
responseDecisions.1.2: Reviewed definition plus two embedded follow-up responses; retained evidence/substantiation categories, nested lists, bridge analogy and car-accident sequence. Explicitly acknowledge implied distinction was overstated; accident remains a hypothetical, not the requested documented actual case. Corrected camera inference and independent corroboration.
responseDecisions.2.1: Preserved three principles/three applications and original paragraph positions. Grounded asymmetry in existing death evidence; removed age, meaningfulness/falsifiability and unusual-claim shortcuts. Withholding belief distinguished from supported denial.
responseDecisions.2.2: Kept original five-part Elvis progression. Qualified razor, identified actual consulted biography rather than claiming autopsy access, bounded survival-evidence claim, corrected negative-proof and consensus exemptions.
responseDecisions.3.1: Retained exact curator transition and four issues/conclusion. Applied burden consistently to asserted existence/nonexistence; distinguished withholding assent/impossibility and expected evidence; Elvis evidence cannot transfer to God case.
responseDecisions.3.2: Preserved nested five-part argument. Repaired simplistic natural/divine simplicity comparison and who-made-God argument; retained skeptical accountability while explicitly requiring reasons for asserted nonexistence.
responseDecisions.4.1: Preserved seven strategies/conclusion; added concrete nonconfrontational reply and evidence-standard reciprocity; no assumption that only affirmative assertions carry burdens.
responseDecisions.4.2: Preserved seven strategies/three reminders; corrected proving-a-negative-impossible heading and response, bounded extraordinary label and clarified suspension versus refutation.
responseDecisions.5.1: Five questions with four options each and five end keys preserved; repaired God scenario ambiguity and false implication that volunteering counterevidence is itself invalid.
responseDecisions.5.2: Five nested four-option questions and five end keys preserved; corrected legal-only definition, Elvis asymmetry, negative-proof claim and always-simplest razor answer.
responseDecisions.6.1: All twelve original discussion questions retained verbatim. They ask open comparisons across law/science/evidence, historical cases, skeptical belief and fallacies, and remain relevant to corrected exposition.
responseDecisions.6.2: All twelve original discussion questions retained verbatim. They test fairness, bias, collaboration, ethics, evidence limits and rhetorical misuse without presupposing disproven answers.

embeddedResponseDecisions.1.1.follow-up-1: Retained five scientific steps; differentiated data from discriminating evidence, peer review from truth and falsifiability from justification.
embeddedResponseDecisions.1.1.follow-up-2: Retained actual Copernican case, corrected circular/elliptical history and Venus evidence compatible with Tycho; no substitute hypothetical drug scenario.
embeddedResponseDecisions.1.2.follow-up-1: Preserved clarification request and corrected earlier implied evidence/substantiation distinction; retained bridge analogy with independence caveat.
embeddedResponseDecisions.1.2.follow-up-2: Preserved concrete car-accident scenario and all nested evidence checks; expressly acknowledged hypothetical instead of claiming an actual sourced incident.
